script.title: Why spacecraft go to die at Point Nemo
sentences: There is a spot in the Pacific Ocean so remote, the nearest humans are often in space.
It is called Point Nemo, about 2,700 kilometres from the closest land.
When the International Space Station passes overhead, its crew is closer than anyone on Earth.
That loneliness makes it perfect for one job: a graveyard for spacecraft.
Since 1971, hundreds of old satellites and cargo ships have been steered down here.
The Russian space station Mir broke apart and sank in this region in 2001.
One day, the International Space Station itself is planned to fall here too.
Would you sail out to the loneliest place on the planet?

script.title: Why a quantum computer is not faster at everything
sentences: Would a quantum computer make every ordinary laptop instantly obsolete?
No, because quantum computing offers possible advantages for particular problems rather than a universal speed boost.
Quantum bits can be manipulated in ways that let algorithms exploit interference between possible computational paths.
Getting a useful answer still requires the right algorithm, enough reliable hardware, and careful management of errors.
Many everyday tasks do not gain a known practical advantage simply by moving onto quantum hardware.
Researchers investigate applications such as simulating quantum systems, where the underlying physics makes these machines especially interesting.
A benchmark result on one carefully chosen task should not be confused with winning at every useful computation.
Would you rather simulate a molecule or speed up a spreadsheet?
